summary: Defines the base SMIng language, a protocol-independent data definition language for management information. Separate documents map it to protocols such as SNMP. It is experimental and not a standard.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 3780 defines SMIng, a language for writing descriptions of the information a network device exposes. A description written in SMIng says what the information is and how it is shaped, but not how to send it, so the same description can be mapped onto SNMP or onto another management protocol.

what is the structure of management information
how does smiing differ from smiv2
subtitle: A data definition language for network management information that does not belong to any one protocol.

tldr.problem: The Structure of Management Information is tied to SNMP and the Structure of Policy Provisioning Information is tied to COPS-PR, so a definition written for one cannot be reused with the other.
tldr.mechanism: SMIng is a data definition language in its own right. It models management information as classes with attributes and events, defines its own base types, and leaves the mapping onto a particular protocol to separate documents.
tldr.outcome: It is an Experimental document. The memo records that the IETF working group aiming to merge SMIv2 and SPPI closed down in April 2003 without consensus, and that the memo was published to record the research group's work.

today: RFC 3780 is an Experimental document from May 2004, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The memo records that the IETF working group set up to replace SMIv2 and SPPI with a single merged language closed down in April 2003, and that this memo and its SNMP mapping companion were published to record the work of the IRTF Network Management Research Group. The security considerations section of the memo is one sentence: the language itself has no security impact on the Internet.

sections.title: Introduction and History
sections.content:
In traditional management systems, management information is viewed as a collection of managed objects in a virtual information store called the Management Information Base. Collections of related objects are defined in MIB modules, written in the Structure of Management Information. SMI version 1 is defined in RFC 1155, RFC 1212 and RFC 1215, and SMI version 2 in RFC 2578, RFC 2579 and RFC 2580, and both are based on adapted subsets of ASN.1. In a similar fashion, policy provisioning information is viewed as a collection of Provisioning Classes and Provisioning Instances in a Policy Information Base, defined in PIB modules written in the Structure of Policy Provisioning Information, which is an adapted subset of SMIv2.

SMIv1 and SMIv2 are bound to SNMP, and SPPI is bound to COPS-PR. Even though the languages have rules in common, it is hard to use common data definitions with both protocols. The purpose of RFC 3780 is to define a common data definition language, named SMIng, that can formally specify data models independent of specific protocols and applications. The appendix defines a core module that supplies common SMIng definitions.

The memo also tells the story. SMIng started in 1999 as a research project to address drawbacks of SMIv2, namely its partial dependence on ASN.1 and a number of exception rules. In 2000 the work moved to the IRTF Network Management Research Group, where it was detailed further. Because the work on COPS-PR and SPPI emerged at the same time, SMIng was split into a core data definition language, which this document defines, and protocol mappings that let the core definitions be applied through more than one management protocol. A companion document holds the SNMP mapping. Another proposal, named SMI Data Structures, was also presented, but neither proposal gathered enough consensus and support, the attempt to merge the existing concepts did not succeed, and the working group closed down in April 2003. The memo and its companion were published to record the work of the research group.
sections.plainLanguage: The problem is that a description written for SNMP cannot be reused with a policy protocol, because each language is bound to its own protocol. SMIng aims to separate the description from the transport. The memo also explains that the effort to merge the two old languages did not succeed, and the working group closed in 2003.

sections.title: How SMIng Models Management Information
sections.content:
SMIng is designed to specify management information in a structured way that is readable both by computer programs such as MIB compilers and by human readers. Management information is modelled in classes. A class can be defined from scratch or by derivation from a parent class, and derivation from multiple parent classes is not possible. Each class has a number of attributes, and each attribute represents an atomic piece of information of a base type, a sub-type of a base type, or another class. Pointers, one of the base types, are references to class instances, to attributes of class instances, or to arbitrary identities.

Related class and type definitions are defined in modules. A module may refer to definitions from other modules by importing identifiers from them. A module may serve one or several purposes: defining management classes, defining events, defining derived types, defining arbitrary untyped identities that serve as values of pointers, defining SMIng extensions so that a module can specify information beyond the scope of the base language in a machine readable notation, and defining information beyond the scope of the base statements based on locally defined or imported extensions. Each module is identified by an upper-case identifier, and the names of all standard modules must be unique, although different versions of the same module should have the same name.

Identifiers are used to name the different kinds of SMIng item, and each identifier is valid in a namespace that depends on the kind of item being defined. The global namespace contains all module identifiers. Each module defines a new namespace that may hold extension, derived type, identity and class identifiers, and each class within a module defines a new namespace that may hold attribute and event identifiers. Each enumeration type and bitset type defines a namespace of its named numbers. Within every namespace each identifier MUST be unique, identifiers MUST NOT exceed 64 characters, and there MUST NOT be any forward references: to refer to an item in the local module its definition must come first, and to refer to an item in another module it must be imported. Where imported identifiers collide with local ones, the ambiguity is resolved by prefixing with the module name and the namespace operator, as in Module::item.
sections.plainLanguage: SMIng describes things as classes. A class holds attributes, and each attribute holds one value of a known shape. Classes can inherit from one parent class, and groups of related classes live in modules that can import names from each other. Every name lives in its own namespace, and names must be defined before they are used.

sections.title: Base Types and Derived Types
sections.content:
SMIng has a set of base types, similar to those of many programming languages but with differences forced by the management information model. Additional types may be defined, derived from those base types or from other derived types, and derived types may use subtyping to formally restrict the set of possible values.

The OctetString base type represents arbitrary binary or textual data. SMIng has a theoretical size limitation of 2 to the 16 minus 1, which is 65535 octets, although module designers should realize there may be implementation and interoperability limitations for sizes in excess of 255 octets. Values are written either as text in double quotes or as a hexadecimal value with an 0x prefix and an even number of at least two digits. A type derived from OctetString may restrict the size in octets by appending a list of sizes or ranges, and the values given must be disjoint and in ascending order.

The Pointer base type represents values that reference class instances, attributes of class instances, or arbitrary identities, and a derived pointer type may be restricted to a specific class, attribute or identity. The ObjectIdentifier base type represents administratively assigned names for use with SNMP and COPS-PR, and the memo says it SHOULD NOT be used in protocol independent SMIng modules, being meant for the SNMP and COPS-PR mappings of attributes of type Pointer. The numeric base types are Integer32, which covers values from -2 to the 31 up to 2 to the 31 minus 1, Integer64, Unsigned32 and Unsigned64, and the floating point base types Float32, Float64 and Float128. Derived numeric types may be restricted by a list of ranges or explicit values, again disjoint and in ascending order.

Two more base types carry named numbers. The Enumeration base type represents values from a set of integers where each value has an assigned name, and the memo recommends that the values be positive, start at 1, be numbered contiguously and be given in ascending order. The Bits base type represents a set of flags identified by small integer numbers starting at 0, each with an assigned name, and negative numbers are forbidden. When a type is derived from an enumeration or a bits type, the set of named numbers may be equal or restricted by removing named numbers, but no named number may be added or changed.
sections.plainLanguage: SMIng has its own set of value shapes: text and binary strings, whole numbers of several widths, floating point numbers, a list of named choices, and a set of named flags. A new type can be made from an existing one by narrowing it, for example allowing only certain lengths of string or only certain number ranges.

sections.title: The SMIng File Structure
sections.content:
The topmost container of SMIng information is a file, which may contain zero, one or more modules. It is RECOMMENDED that modules be stored in separate files named after them where possible, though collecting several modules in one file can be reasonable for dedicated purposes. The top level construct is the module statement, which takes an upper-case module name and a statement block containing sections of definitions in an obligatory order.

That order is: optional import statements, then the mandatory organization, contact and description statements, then an optional reference statement, then at least one mandatory revision statement, then optional extension statements, optional typedef statements, optional identity statements and optional class statements. The first part is the module's meta information, describing the module as a whole, and the rest holds the main definitions.

The grammar rests on statements. Each statement starts with a lower-case keyword followed by zero or more arguments, and an argument may be quoted text, an identifier, a value of any base type, a list of identifiers in parentheses, or a statement block in curly braces. Because statement blocks are valid arguments, statement sequences can be nested, and each statement ends with a semicolon. Comments may appear anywhere except between the characters of a single token, and they start with a pair of adjacent slashes and run to the end of the line; it is RECOMMENDED that substantive descriptions be placed in a description clause instead, so that parsers can find them. Textual arguments are enclosed in double quotes, and a backslash introduces an escape for a newline, a tab, a double quote or another backslash. Where a line break is followed by whitespace used to indent the text, that whitespace is stripped.

At any place where a statement is expected but an unknown lower-case word is read, the statements MUST be skipped up to the proper semicolon, including nested statement blocks. This is what lets a parser handle a file that uses extensions it does not know.
sections.plainLanguage: A SMIng file holds modules, and each module holds a fixed sequence of sections: what it imports, who wrote it, what it is, its revisions, and then its extensions, types, identities and classes. A parser that meets a statement it does not recognise skips to the end of it, so unknown extensions do not stop it reading the rest.

sections.title: Classes, Attributes and Events
sections.content:
The class statement defines a new class, which is a container of related attributes and events. A class is defined either from scratch or derived from a parent class, and a derived class inherits all the attributes and events of its parent and can add more. The statement takes an upper-case class identifier and a block of detailed information in an obligatory order.

An attribute gets a name and a block of details. Its type statement must be present and names either a type or a class, and a type name may be restricted by a second argument. The access statement must be present for attributes typed by a base type or a derived type and must be absent for attributes typed by a class. It gives the maximal level of access, independently of any administrative authorization policy, and takes one of three values: readwrite, where read and write access make sense, readonly, where write access is never possible, and eventonly, where the object is accessible only through an event. These are ordered from least to greatest access. The default statement gives an acceptable default value, a hint to implementors that overrides the default of the underlying type. The format statement hints how the value might be displayed, and units names the units of the value.

The unique statement, which need not be present, takes a comma-separated list of attributes that together make up a unique identification of all possible instances of the class, and it can be used as a unique key in the underlying protocol. If the list is empty the class is a scalar class with a single instance. If the statement is absent the class is not meant to be instantiated directly, but to be contained in other classes or to be the parent of other classes. The event statement defines an event related to an instance of the class that can occur asynchronously, and takes a lower-case event identifier and a block of details.
sections.plainLanguage: A class holds the values that describe one kind of thing and the events that thing can raise. Each value says its type, whether it can be read, written or only seen through an event, and optionally its default value and units. A class can name the attributes that together identify one instance of it.

sections.title: Extending a Module and the Language
sections.content:
The memo sets rules for revising a module. Changes are not allowed if they have any potential to cause interoperability problems between an implementation using the original specification and one using an updated specification. A new revision statement must be added in front of the existing revision statements, and any necessary changes applied to the organization and contact statements. A module name MUST NOT be changed, except to correct typographical errors, and definitions MUST NOT be moved from one module to another. Obsolete definitions MUST NOT be removed, since their identifiers may still be referenced by other modules.

Within those limits a definition may be revised in several ways: named numbers may be added to an Enumeration or Bits type; a type may be replaced by another type derived from the same base type with the same set of values and identical semantics; a class may be replaced by another class derived from the same base class with identical semantics; a status may move from current to deprecated and then to obsolete; a default or a units statement may be added or updated; a class may be given new attributes; and clarifications may be added to a description statement. Anything else, meaning any change to the semantics of a previous definition, MUST be achieved by a new definition with a new identifier, and a class whose attributes change semantically can be defined by derivation from the old class with the changed attributes refined. Changing the identifier associated with an existing definition counts as a semantic change, because those strings may be used in an import statement.

The language itself is also extensible. The extension statement declares a new statement, optionally with a formal ABNF grammar, and the memo explains that this lets a parser tell known extensions from unknown ones, complain about unknown statements such as typos, complain about wrong usage when it can read the ABNF, distinguish extensions from different organizations that happen to share a name, and state clearly which extensions an implementation supports. The formal effect of an extension statement is only to declare its existence and status, and optionally its grammar; the semantics, the contexts in which it may be used, and the circumstances in which it is mandatory or optional belong in the description statement. The memo names the formal SNMP mapping as an extension, and suggests vendor annotations of definitions as a possible use.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo is careful about when a module may change. Anything that would change the meaning of an existing definition needs a new name instead, so that modules already written keep working. New kinds of statement can be added by declaring an extension, which lets a parser recognise the ones it knows and skip the rest.

items.title: OctetString
items.text: Arbitrary binary or textual data, with a theoretical limit of 65535 octets.

items.title: Pointer
items.text: A reference to a class instance, an attribute of one, or an arbitrary identity.

items.title: ObjectIdentifier
items.text: Administratively assigned names for SNMP and COPS-PR; not for protocol independent modules.

items.title: Integer32, Integer64, Unsigned32, Unsigned64
items.text: Whole numbers of four different widths, each with its own range.

items.title: Float32, Float64, Float128
items.text: Floating point numbers in three widths.

items.title: Enumeration
items.text: A set of integers where each value carries an assigned name.

items.title: Bits
items.text: A set of flags, each identified by a bit number and a name.
